title: Probation-router for heterogeneous model candidates with confidence calibration and staged failover
creator: Sofia Chen
description:
Goal: Implement a probation-stage routing component that probes lower-cost model variants (and kernel configurations) early in the request lifecycle, uses a calibrated confidence metric to accept or reject the speculative candidate, and falls back gracefully to the primary decode path when acceptance is low. The router should minimize added latency for accepted requests while ensuring false-accepts remain negligible for customer-facing outputs.

Scope: runtime library + router policy + rollout tooling. Does NOT include new model training or new quantization formats. Focus areas: prefill probe design, confidence calibration (statistical and ML-based), per-request kernel-selection hints, KV-cache warmup heuristics, and console rollouts with per-route observability.

Motivation: We can save GPU cycles and reduce p99 latency for many requests by opportunistically decoding on cheaper model kernels or quantized variants when we are confident the output will match the primary model's behavior. Current speculative approaches in the codebase are decoder-first; this work adds a short probation probe phase (bounded tokens) with an explicit acceptance metric and observable rollback path to reduce regressions and customer impact.
acceptance_criteria: Router can issue a bounded-length probe (<= 8 tokens) on a candidate model/kernel pair and compute an acceptance score within 2ms of probe completion
Calibrated acceptance score thresholds chosen such that end-to-end false_accept_rate <= 0.3% on sampled production traffic (verified in simulation)
When accepted, the end-to-end p99 latency for compatible requests is reduced by >= 5% compared to baseline (no probation) without increasing GPU cost per token by more than 3%
Fallback execution runs automatically and preserves per-request KV cache consistency; no user-visible corruption reported in staged canary (0 incidents in 1k canary requests)
Router exposes per-route telemetry: probe_latency_ms, acceptance_score, accepted_rate, fallback_rate, and false_accept_rate to Console dashboards
Unit and integration tests for router logic, calibration util, and KV-warmup applied with >= 90% code coverage for new modules
Feature gate + canary rollout configured in Console and associated rollout playbook documented in Confluence
implementation_milestones: Spec draft and design review complete (this ticket)
Simulation harness to replay 72h production traces and compute acceptance ROC curves
Runtime integration: lightweight probe API + routing policy module
Calibration job: offline calibration and online continuous calibration regimen
technical_notes: Probe strategy: issue a short prefill-like probe (max 8 tokens) on candidate model variants using the same input context but with reduced scheduling priority and dedicated kernel hints
Acceptance signal candidates: token-level logprob delta vs primary model, token entropy ratio, aggregate KL divergence across probe tokens, and sequence-level length-normalized score
Calibration approach: offline supervised calibration using production-labeled pairs (primary vs candidate) + isotonic regression to map raw score -> calibrated probability
Kernel selection hinting: router suggests preferred kernel/quantization for candidate runs; runtime uses kernel fingerprint to pick low-latency execution path when available
KV-warmup: when probe accepts, router issues a warmup handoff to the primary pool to reuse probe KV where compatible, otherwise discard probe KV to avoid pollution

Failure modes: probe-hook cold start (higher probe latency), probe producing divergent context (mismatch in tokenization/transformer config), and resource starvation for probe tasks — mitigation via backpressure and admission control

Safety: acceptance thresholds are conservative initially; any candidate acceptance requires both calibrated score >= threshold AND a per-request consistency check (e.g., no top-1 token flip in first 2 probe tokens)
testing_plan: Replay-based evaluation: run the probe algorithm over a 1M-request sample (sanitized PII) to compute ROC, PR, and expected cost savings
A/B canary: 5% traffic split for 72 hours with verbose logging; compare hallucination/regression signals against control
Microbenchmarks: measure probe latency overhead and kernel-switch cost across GPU families (A100, H100) and quantized kernels
Chaos tests: force probe pool eviction/failure and ensure fallback path completes within SLA
End-to-end fuzzing: randomized token sequences to detect rare KV corruption or race conditions
rollout_plan: Stage 1: internal canary (dev cluster) — 100% internal traffic for 2 days
Stage 2: 5% external traffic for 72 hours with alerting on false_accept_rate and p99 latency
Stage 3: 25% traffic with automated rollback if any high-severity regression
Stage 4: global rollout with adaptive threshold adjustment enabled
comments: 2026-03-01 - Sofia Chen: Created initial spec and goals. Decided on bounded probe length (<=8) after estimating KV-warmup cost vs benefit.

2026-03-05 - Daniel Park: Ran initial simulation on 200k requests; preliminary calibrated threshold at 0.92 yields ~6% p99 savings with 0.6% false_accept_rate. Need tighter threshold and additional features to reduce false accepts.

2026-03-08 - Priya Nair (Review): Reviewed calibration approach; suggested adding isotonic regression and a per-route override to tighten thresholds for high-risk customers. Also flagged need for explicit telemetry exposure in Console.

2026-03-10 - Daniel Park: Implemented probe API prototype and kernel-hint plumbing. Microbenchmarks show probe overhead of ~1.8ms on H100 when kinsh=fast-kernel. Noted increased scheduling jitter under heavy load; added admission control idea to spec.
2026-03-12 - Security (Alex Ruiz): Confirmed that probe data is processed inline and not logged to persistent stores; requested KMS annotation if probes are retained for calibration longer than 24h.

2026-03-14 - Daniel Park: Integration tests green for basic acceptance path. Next: finalize calibration job and schedule 72h replay run. Open question: where to store continuous calibration artifacts (S3 vs internal DB) — prefer S3 for reproducibility.
